https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce34.text: Image source, Reuters By Samantha Granville Â and Â Alys Davies Published 11 August 2026, 10:42 BST Updated 2 hours ago A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war. It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to Moscow with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power. Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He had been put on trial and appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence. Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule. In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces. That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year. Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death". The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell. The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij. Image source, NurPhoto via GettyImages Image caption, Atef Najib appeared in a cage in court during his sentencing on Tuesday Nouha al-Masri has spent 15 years waiting for this moment. She is not just part of the five person prosecution team, she is also a plaintiff in this case. Masri lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at Al-Omari Square in Deraa. "The verdict reflects the magnitude of the sacrifices we made, the sacrifices of the martyrs, the suffering and pain of the victims, the missing, and the detainees," she told the BBC. "We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us." For Masri, the verdict is a new chapter. "Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward." Syria trial seen as first step on long road for Assad's victims Published 29 April The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding Published 3 days ago Calls for justice and accountability in Syria grow after Assad's fall Published 6 January 2025 It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow. It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership. An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture. He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty. Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia. Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions. Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994. Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies. Much of his rule was defined by the civil war. Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus. Beállítom Elszáradt napraforgó és kukorica, kiszáradt termőföldek látszanak azokon a fotókon, amelyeket az Arad megyei mezőgazdasági igazgatóság vezetője, Adrian Alda tett közzé . A képek a magyar–román határ romániai oldalán, többek között Nagylak környékén készültek, de a sorozatba bekerült egy fotó a Békés megyei Mezőhegyesről is. Alda szerint egyes földeken már nem egyszerűen gyengébb termésről van szó: a kár eléri a 90 százalékot, néhol pedig megközelíti a 100 százalékot . Augusztus 25-ig 995 bejelentés érkezett az aszály miatt károsodott tavaszi vetésekről, összesen 23 122 hektárról. A legsúlyosabban a kukoricát és a napraforgót érintette a szárazság, de lucerna-, cukorrépa-, szója- és zöldségföldeken, illetve szőlőkben is jelentettek károkat. Különösen sok bejelentés érkezett Arad megye nyugati, Magyarországhoz közeli részéről. A kárfelmérés még tart, így a mostani adatok nem jelentik a végső mérleget. A határ magyar oldalán sem sokkal jobb a helyzet. A HungaroMet hétfői értékelése szerint az Alföldön az elmúlt harminc napban sokfelé 10 milliméternél is kevesebb csapadék hullott, a kukorica és a napraforgó pedig javarészt már elszáradt. Az ország nagy részén a talaj továbbra is rendkívül száraz, a múlt heti esők csak kisebb területeken enyhítették az aszályt. Arad megyében ráadásul nem a tavaszi növényekkel kezdődött a probléma. A gazdák korábban már közel 80 ezer hektárnyi őszi vetésben is jelentettek aszálykárt, a helyszíni felméréseken 30–70 százalék közötti károsodást állapítottak meg. Alda szerint Arad 2026-ban az aszály által legsúlyosabban érintett romániai megyék közé tartozik. A szárazság jóval nagyobb térséget érint a határ menti Arad megyénél. Magyarországon főleg az Alföldön alakult ki súlyos mezőgazdasági aszály, Romániában pedig a Bánságban, a Körösvidéken, Máramarosban és Erdély nagy részén is jelentős a vízhiány az öntözetlen kukoricaföldeken. A román meteorológiai szolgálat szerint a száraz talaj és a magas hőmérséklet miatt sárgulnak és száradnak a növények, felgyorsul az érés, ami a termés mennyiségét és minőségét is rontja. A helyzet régiónként eltérő, de a magyar Alföldtől Partiumon át Erdélyig ugyanannak a hosszan tartó száraz és forró időszaknak a következményei látszanak. Photograph: MBI/Alamy View image in fullscreen A woman who had just arrived in the UK from Iran and had been placed in a hotel near Heathrow by the Home Office said she was raped by a security guard at the hotel. Photograph: MBI/Alamy Violence against women and girls Female asylum seekers report being sexually assaulted by British men Women say they are too fearful to pursue criminal prosecution of rapes, for fear of having their claims refused Diane Taylor Sun 13 Sep 2026 05.14 EDT Last modified on Sun 13 Sep 2026 05.46 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Female asylum seekers are reporting rapes and sexual assaults by British men but many say they are too fearful to pursue criminal prosecutions. Their voices are rarely heard but some have spoken to the Guardian at a time when the far right is intensifying tropes about endemic rape of English women and girls by “fighting age” male asylum seekers. The rallying cry by far-right agitator Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, to motivate his black balaclava-clad followers last weekend when they protested about the arrival of asylum seekers in Dover and Portsmouth, focused almost exclusively on unsubstantiated claims of widespread rape perpetrated by asylum seekers. While there have been a handful of convictions of asylum seekers for serious sexual offences, which have attracted widespread media coverage, there is no comprehensive published data about crimes committed by asylum seekers. One woman, who spent two years in an asylum hotel after fleeing religious persecution and domestic violence, said she was repeatedly verbally and physically harassed by a staff member at the hotel she was accommodated in. This included unwanted touching and holding on to her hands when handing over documents. After a while he started visiting her room regularly, asking her out for drinks and on dates. He took her number from the hotel database and started texting her repeatedly from his personal phone asking for sex. At that point she reported him to hotel staff and was moved to another hotel. “It was awful,” she said. “He told me he wanted to have sex with me.” In another case, a woman who had just arrived in the UK from Iran and had been placed in a hotel near Heathrow by the Home Office , said she was raped by a security guard at her hotel. “It was very terrifying. I didn’t know what to do. I reported the attack to the hotel staff and I was asked if I wanted to make a statement to the police. I did not know if the police here would be like the police in Iran, so I was too scared to do anything. “I was also worried that if I reported the rape it would make it more likely that my asylum claim would be refused.” She was moved to another hotel soon after reporting the rape and does not know what happened to the perpetrator. In a third case, a lesbian asylum seeker from Uganda whose asylum claim was based on fear of imprisonment or death in her home country if her sexual orientation was discovered, was unable to find a legal aid lawyer to represent her. “I managed to find a private immigration lawyer but I had no money to pay him, so he forced me to have sex with him as a form of payment even though he knew what my asylum case was,” she said. “I felt there was nothing I could do to prevent this.” All three women were later granted refugee status. It is likely that incidents of sexual assault and rape of asylum seekers are under-reported to Home Office accommodation contractors. A home affairs select committee inquiry into asylum accommodation heard evidence about inadequate safeguarding in asylum accommodation. The British Red Cross told the inquiry that this lack of safeguarding had placed “extraordinary strain” on their frontline refugee support teams. They provided examples including a staff member at a hotel trying to use a key card to get into a woman’s room late one night when she was taking a bath. They referred to a “pervasive culture of sexual harassment” in one hotel, including instances of sexual assault. A spokesperson from Women for Refugee Women, which supports women in the asylum system, said: “The weaponisation of violence against women and girls by far-right groups does nothing to make women safer. It distorts the reality of abuse, creates barriers to support and justice for survivors, and allows perpetrators to hide behind racist stereotypes instead of being held accountable. “Using violence against women and girls to demonise people seeking safety here is a dangerous distraction. This violence is a systemic problem, not one confined to any nationality or immigration status, and it must urgently be treated as one.” Ciara Bergman, chief executive of Rape Crisis England & Wales said: “We remain seriously concerned about a lack of appropriate safeguards in place to protect women seeking asylum in the UK from sexual violence, abuse and exploitation. “This cohort of women and girls are particularly vulnerable to sexual abuse and exploitation. Many have limited or no information about their rights at all, let alone meaningful avenues through which to enforce them. “Our government has committed to halving violence against women and girls in a decade; it is vital that this includes those seeking asylum and living within the asylum complex.” Home Office sources said there is published guidance about issues of this kind in Home Office accommodation known as the statement of requirements for asylum accommodation and support. The guidance states: “This would typically include assessing any immediate risk to the alleged victim and others, considering what support services may be required, and determining whether any protective measures are necessary.” Explore more on these topics Violence against women and girls Immigration and asylum Rape and sexual assault Sexual harassment Refugees Home Office news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland
